angle: old money vs new money, 20 differences from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: Old Money vs New Money: 20 Differences

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. There are two kinds of rich in America. There's old money, families who have been wealthy for generations, quietly, often without anyone noticing. And there's new money, people who made their fortune themselves, often fast, and often very visibly. They both have money. But they tend to think about it, spend it and protect it very differently. Today, twenty differences between old money and new money, and the lessons you can steal from both, whatever your bank balance looks like.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's a number you'll hear a lot in wealth management. A widely cited study by the Williams Group found that about seventy percent of wealthy families lose their wealth by the second generation, and about ninety percent by the third.

card.note: Williams Group research, widely cited and debated

scenes.short_hook: Most family fortunes vanish by the third generation. Here's why.

scenes.text: That research is debated, and different studies measure it differently. But the pattern is so common it has an old saying. Shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves in three generations. The first generation builds the fortune in work shirts. The second enjoys it. The third is back in shirtsleeves. Old money families are, by definition, the ones who broke that pattern. That's why their habits are worth studying.
scenes.caption: SHIRTSLEEVES TO SHIRTSLEEVES

scenes.text: We'll compare old and new money from three angles. First, the numbers. How each group earns, invests, borrows and handles taxes. Second, the psychology. How they think about status, risk, time and identity. And third, the playbook. The practical systems old money families use to keep wealth for generations, and the strengths new money brings that old money often lacks. I want to be clear. These are broad patterns, not rules. Plenty of individuals break the stereotypes in both directions.
scenes.query: Old mansion and modern glass house
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And the first difference is about where the money actually comes from.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our sources. Family wealth transfer research comes from the Williams Group, published in the book Preparing Heirs by Roy Williams and Vic Preisser. Billionaire data comes from UBS's Billionaire Ambitions reports. Millionaire profiles come from Ramsey Solutions' National Study of Millionaires and Thomas Stanley's research. The Vanderbilt story comes from the book Fortune's Children by Arthur T. Vanderbilt the second. Tax rules come from the IRS. This is education, not financial advice, and not tax or legal advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven financial differences between old money and new money.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Difference number one. Old money lives on assets. New money often lives on income.

card.title: Assets vs income
card.sub: money that works vs money that's earned

scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 1

scenes.text: Many new money fortunes come from a high income or a single big event, like selling a company, a big contract or a successful career in sports or entertainment. That money arrives as cash, and it's easy to spend. Old money families, by contrast, typically live on what their assets produce. Rents, dividends, interest and business profits. The core assets stay untouched, and only part of the income is spent.
scenes.caption: ASSETS VS INCOME

scenes.text: That's a crucial difference. If you spend from income, a job loss or a bad year can end everything. If you spend only part of what your assets produce, the wealth can keep growing even while you live on it. Many old money families follow a version of this rule for decades. Spend some of the returns, never the principal.
scenes.caption: SPEND RETURNS, NOT PRINCIPAL

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Start building assets that produce income, like index funds, a retirement account, a rental property or a small business. Over time, aim for a day when part of your living costs are covered by what your assets earn, not just by what you earn.
scenes.caption: BUILD INCOME ASSETS

scenes.text: Here's a simple way to picture it. Imagine two people who each have two million dollars. One spends it like income, buying a bigger house and better cars. The other invests it and spends only a small share of what it earns each year. Twenty years later, the first person may have very little left, while the second person may have more than they started with, and has been living on it the whole time.
scenes.caption: SAME MONEY, DIFFERENT FUTURE

scenes.text: Difference number two. Old money thinks in generations. New money often thinks in years.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 2

scenes.text: When you've just made your fortune, the natural questions are about the next few years. What should I buy? How do I enjoy this? Old money families often frame decisions around decades and generations. Will this still matter for our grandchildren? That longer view changes everything, from how they invest to how they spend.
scenes.caption: GENERATIONS VS YEARS

scenes.text: A long time horizon makes compounding work at full strength. Money invested for fifty years, or for multiple lifetimes, can grow enormously, even at modest returns. It also makes families more patient with market drops, because a bad year is a tiny part of a hundred year plan.
scenes.caption: A HUNDRED YEAR PLAN

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Stretch your time horizon. When you invest, think in decades, not months. Ask yourself what decision your seventy year old self would thank you for.
scenes.caption: THINK IN DECADES

scenes.text: Endowments at some of the oldest American universities show what a very long horizon can do. Funds that spend only a small share each year, and reinvest the rest, have grown over generations into some of the largest pools of money in the world. The principle works at any scale. Patience plus a modest spending rate lets money outlive the people who saved it.
scenes.caption: THE ENDOWMENT MODEL

scenes.text: Difference number three. Old money spreads its bets. New money is often concentrated.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 3

scenes.text: New fortunes are frequently built by concentration. A founder owns a huge stake in one company. An athlete has one skill that pays enormously. Concentration is how many fortunes are made. But it's also how many are lost, when a single company or career declines.
scenes.caption: CONCENTRATED

scenes.text: Old money families tend to diversify across many assets. Stocks, bonds, real estate, private businesses and more. They accept that diversification may mean they won't get the very highest returns, in exchange for protecting the wealth from any single disaster. Their goal is not to get rich. It's to stay rich. As one saying in wealth management puts it, concentration builds wealth, and diversification protects it.
scenes.caption: SPREAD THE BETS

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Concentration can build wealth, for example in your own career or business. But once you have savings, spread them out. Broad low cost index funds are a simple way for ordinary investors to own small pieces of many companies.
scenes.caption: STAY RICH

scenes.text: Think of a founder whose entire net worth is in one company's stock. If that company thrives, they become even richer. If it collapses, as many once famous companies have, their fortune can collapse with it. Old money families have usually lived through enough cycles to know that no single company, industry or country stays on top forever.
scenes.caption: NOTHING STAYS ON TOP FOREVER

scenes.text: Difference number four. How they use debt.

card.title: Debt as a tool vs debt as a lifestyle

scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 4
scenes.chapter: 4. Debt as a tool vs debt as a lifestyle

scenes.text: Some new money spends on visible things with borrowed money. Luxury cars on loans, huge mortgages on show homes, big credit lines. When income drops, that debt becomes dangerous. Many famous athletes and entertainers who went broke had large debts tied to their lifestyle.
scenes.caption: DEBT FOR LIFESTYLE
scenes.short_hook: The rich use debt very differently than everyone else.

scenes.text: Old money families, when they borrow, tend to borrow against assets for specific purposes, often at low rates, and rarely for consumption. Some wealthy families borrow against their investment portfolios instead of selling, which can have tax advantages. But that strategy carries real risks and only makes sense with large, diversified assets and careful planning.
scenes.caption: DEBT AS A TOOL

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Avoid borrowing for things that lose value. If you do borrow, borrow for things that can grow or produce income, keep the debt manageable, and know exactly what it costs.
scenes.caption: BORROW FOR ASSETS

scenes.text: History is full of examples. Many professional athletes earn more in a few years than most people earn in a lifetime, yet a widely cited Sports Illustrated report in two thousand nine claimed that a large share of former NFL and NBA players faced financial stress within a few years of retiring. Whatever the exact share, the pattern is familiar. Big income, big lifestyle, big debts, and then the income stops.
scenes.caption: WHEN THE INCOME STOPS

scenes.text: Difference number five. Old money plans for taxes years ahead.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 5

scenes.text: Many people with new money get a painful surprise at tax time, especially after selling a company or receiving a large payout. Old money families typically work with tax professionals and plan years ahead, using legal strategies like retirement accounts, charitable giving, trusts and careful timing of sales.
scenes.caption: PLAN AHEAD

scenes.text: One well known rule is the step up in basis. Under current US tax law, when someone inherits certain assets like stocks, the cost basis is generally reset to the value at the time of death. That can greatly reduce capital gains taxes for heirs. Laws change, and details matter, so families work with professionals on this.
scenes.caption: LEGAL STRATEGIES

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. You don't need a family office to plan for taxes. Use tax advantaged retirement accounts, understand how long you hold investments before selling, and keep good records. A little planning can save a lot.
scenes.caption: USE TAX ADVANTAGED ACCOUNTS

scenes.text: For regular families, the same mindset shows up in simple choices. Contributing to a four oh one k before taxes, using a Roth IRA for tax free growth, holding investments more than a year so gains may qualify for lower long term capital gains rates, and keeping receipts and records. None of it is glamorous, but over a lifetime it can add up to a large amount of money kept instead of paid.
scenes.caption: BORING BUT POWERFUL

scenes.text: Difference number six. How much they spend.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 6

scenes.text: New money can spend at a pace that outruns even a large fortune. Big houses, staff, cars, travel and gifts for friends and family. The fortune feels endless, until it isn't. Stories of lottery winners and athletes who went broke are common because big sudden wealth often comes with big sudden spending.
scenes.caption: SPENDING TOO FAST

scenes.text: Many old money families follow a spending discipline. Some foundations and endowments, for example, aim to spend around four to five percent of their assets each year, so the principal can keep up with inflation over time. Families that last often follow something similar.
scenes.caption: A SPENDING DISCIPLINE

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Know your spending rate. What share of your income do you spend? What share of your investments would you need to withdraw to live? Keeping that number sustainable is how wealth survives.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR RATE

scenes.text: Think about lottery winners. Many receive a fortune overnight, with no experience managing large sums, and with friends and family suddenly asking for help. Researchers studying lottery winners in Florida found that larger winners were less likely to file for bankruptcy in the short term, but that over time the protective effect faded considerably. Sudden money without a spending discipline is fragile.
scenes.caption: SUDDEN MONEY IS FRAGILE

scenes.text: Difference number seven. How they protect wealth.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 7

scenes.text: Old money families often use legal structures, like trusts, family partnerships and insurance, to protect wealth from lawsuits, divorce, poor decisions and taxes. These structures can also control how heirs receive money, for example in stages rather than all at once.
scenes.caption: PROTECTING WEALTH

scenes.text: New money is often more exposed. Assets may sit in one person's name, without a will or estate plan. Surveys have found that many Americans, including many with significant assets, don't have a will. That leaves families vulnerable to court processes and conflicts.
scenes.caption: EXPOSED WITHOUT A PLAN

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. At minimum, have a will, name beneficiaries on every account, and carry enough insurance, including liability coverage. If you have significant assets or young children, talk to an estate planning attorney.
scenes.caption: THE BASICS FOR EVERYONE

scenes.text: It's also about protecting heirs from themselves. A twenty year old who suddenly inherits millions with no guidance is at real risk. Structures that release money gradually, or that require a trustee's approval for big withdrawals, can give young heirs time to grow up before they're handed the keys to everything.
scenes.caption: PROTECTING HEIRS FROM THEMSELVES

scenes.text: Here's what happens when new money never learns these lessons. Cornelius Vanderbilt built one of the largest fortunes in American history in the eighteen hundreds, through shipping and railroads. When he died in eighteen seventy seven, he was among the richest people in the country.
scenes.caption: CORNELIUS VANDERBILT
scenes.short_hook: The richest family in America lost almost everything. Here's how.

scenes.text: His descendants built enormous mansions on Fifth Avenue and in Newport, and spent on a scale that's hard to imagine. According to the book Fortune's Children, written by a Vanderbilt descendant, the fortune was largely gone within a few generations. At a family reunion in nineteen seventy three, the book says, not one of the gathered descendants was a millionaire.
scenes.caption: THE FORTUNE DISAPPEARED

scenes.text: Compare that with families like the Rockefellers, who used trusts, family offices, philanthropy and strong family governance. Their wealth has lasted far longer. The difference wasn't how much money they started with. It was the systems they built around it.
scenes.caption: SYSTEMS, NOT SIZE

scenes.text: That's angle one. Assets versus income, generations versus years, diversification, how they use debt, tax planning, spending rate and protection. Now angle two. The psychology. Because the biggest differences between old and new money are in their heads.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Money changes how people feel, and how they want others to see them. New wealth often comes with something to prove. Old wealth often comes with something to protect. Those two mindsets lead to very different behavior.
scenes.caption: PROVE VS PROTECT

scenes.text: Difference number eight. Old money tends to be quiet. New money is often loud.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 8

scenes.text: Big logos, flashy cars and social media displays are more common with new wealth. Old money families often prefer discretion. Unbranded clothing, older cars, understated homes. This style is sometimes called quiet luxury or stealth wealth.
scenes.caption: LOUD
scenes.short_hook: Old money whispers. New money shouts. Here's the difference.

scenes.text: There are practical reasons for being quiet. Visible wealth attracts scammers, lawsuits, and people who want something. It can also create resentment. Old money families often teach their children not to discuss money outside the family.
scenes.caption: QUIET LUXURY

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. You don't need to show what you have. Privacy protects you, and it frees you from the pressure to keep up appearances. Let your accounts grow quietly.
scenes.caption: PRIVACY PROTECTS

scenes.text: There's a famous phrase sometimes used to describe this attitude. Money talks, wealth whispers. Whether or not anyone can prove who said it first, it captures the idea well. Those who have had wealth for a long time often see no reason to announce it. For them, the real luxury is privacy, time and freedom, none of which come with a logo.
scenes.caption: MONEY TALKS, WEALTH WHISPERS

scenes.text: Difference number nine. Old money buys quality. New money often buys brands.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 9

scenes.text: Old money families often value well made items that last for decades, even generations. Furniture, watches, clothing and homes that are maintained and passed down. New money is more likely to chase the newest and most recognized brands.
scenes.caption: BUYING TO KEEP

scenes.text: Buying quality to keep is often cheaper over time. A well made item used for thirty years costs very little per year. A trendy item replaced every season costs a fortune.
scenes.caption: CHASING BRANDS

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. For things you use daily, buy quality and take care of it. Skip trends. Ask whether you'd still want this item in ten years.
scenes.caption: TEN YEAR TEST

scenes.text: You can see this in the idea of heirloom quality. A good wool coat, a solid wood table, a leather bag that ages well. These items are often bought once and repaired rather than replaced. Over decades, the cost per year can be lower than buying cheaper versions again and again. It's frugality and elegance at the same time.
scenes.caption: HEIRLOOM QUALITY

scenes.text: Difference number ten. Old money feels secure. New money often feels the need to prove itself.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 10

scenes.text: When you grow up with wealth, you don't need to show it to feel successful. When you've just made it, especially after growing up without money, there can be a strong urge to show the world you've arrived.
scenes.caption: NOTHING TO PROVE

scenes.text: That urge is human and understandable. But it's expensive. Buying things to prove something to others is a race with no finish line, because there's always someone with more.
scenes.caption: THE URGE TO SHOW

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Find your security in your balance sheet, your skills and your relationships, not in what other people see.
scenes.caption: SECURITY ON THE BALANCE SHEET

scenes.text: Psychologists have long observed that people often use possessions to signal identity and status, especially when they feel insecure about their position. That's not a moral failing. It's very human. But knowing it gives you a choice. Next time you feel the urge to buy something to show others, ask whether you'd still want it if nobody would ever see it.
scenes.caption: WOULD YOU BUY IT IF NOBODY SAW?

scenes.text: Difference number eleven. Old money is patient. New money often moves fast.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 11

scenes.text: Many new fortunes were built with speed, fast growth, bold bets, quick decisions. That works well when you're building. But when it comes to protecting wealth, speed can be dangerous. Quick investments in exciting opportunities are how many fortunes shrink.
scenes.caption: SPEED

scenes.text: Old money tends to move slowly. Long due diligence, long holding periods, and a willingness to miss out on hot trends. They often sound boring, and that's the point.
scenes.caption: PATIENCE

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. When it comes to your savings, slow down. Be suspicious of urgency. Good investments rarely require you to decide today.
scenes.caption: SLOW DOWN

scenes.text: Old money investors often talk about having time on their side. They don't need to make a fortune this year, because they already have one. That frees them to wait for good opportunities, and to say no to most pitches. For regular investors, the same mindset helps. You don't need to get rich this year. You need to stay invested for the next thirty.
scenes.caption: TIME ON THEIR SIDE

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free and it helps us keep making long, honest videos about money. Okay, difference twelve.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Difference number twelve. Old money invests in relationships.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 12

scenes.text: Old money families often maintain long relationships with advisors, lawyers, bankers and other families, sometimes across generations. These networks provide trusted advice, opportunities and protection.
scenes.caption: RELATIONSHIPS COMPOUND

scenes.text: New money may move from advisor to advisor, or rely on whoever pitches them first. That can lead to bad advice and high fees. Trust takes time to build, and it compounds like money.
scenes.caption: TRUSTED ADVICE

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Build long term relationships with trustworthy professionals and mentors. Look for fiduciaries, people legally required to act in your best interest.
scenes.caption: FIND A FIDUCIARY

scenes.text: For ordinary people, this can be as simple as finding one trusted tax preparer, one good insurance agent, and perhaps one fee only financial planner, and sticking with them for years. Over time, they learn your situation, and you learn whether you can trust their advice. That kind of relationship is worth more than any single tip.
scenes.caption: ONE TRUSTED TEAM

scenes.text: Difference number thirteen. Old money families often build identity around values, not wealth.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 13

scenes.text: Families that keep wealth for generations often emphasize shared values, like education, service, work ethic and philanthropy. Money is seen as a tool to support those values, not the identity itself.
scenes.caption: VALUES FIRST

scenes.text: When identity is tied only to money, people can make reckless decisions to protect their status. When identity is tied to values, money decisions become clearer.
scenes.caption: MONEY SUPPORTS VALUES

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Write down what your family stands for. Let those values guide spending and saving decisions.
scenes.caption: WHAT WE STAND FOR

scenes.text: This is also why old money families often encourage meaningful work, even for heirs who don't need the income. Work gives purpose, identity and skills. Heirs who find meaningful roles, in a family business, a career or philanthropy, are often far more likely to preserve wealth than those who drift without direction.
scenes.caption: PURPOSE BEYOND MONEY

scenes.text: Difference number fourteen. New money takes big risks. Old money manages risk.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 14

scenes.text: This is where new money has a real strength. Building a fortune usually requires taking risks. Starting a company, changing careers, betting on yourself. Many old money heirs, raised to protect wealth, become too cautious to build anything new.
scenes.caption: BUILDERS TAKE RISKS

scenes.text: The best approach often combines both. Take smart risks with your career and a small part of your money, while protecting the core of your wealth with diversification and insurance.
scenes.caption: KEEPERS MANAGE RISK

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Separate your money into two buckets. A protected core, and a small amount for calculated risks you understand.
scenes.caption: CORE AND RISK

scenes.text: Many self made fortunes were built by people who put almost everything on one idea. But once the fortune exists, the smartest builders often change strategy and start acting like keepers. They sell part of their concentrated position, diversify, and protect the downside. Building and keeping really are two different skills.
scenes.caption: BUILDING AND KEEPING ARE DIFFERENT

scenes.text: That's angle two. Quiet versus loud, quality versus brands, security versus proving, patience versus speed, networks, identity and risk. Now angle three. The playbook. How old money keeps it, and what new money does better.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Keeping wealth for generations doesn't happen by accident. It takes systems. The families that last often share a handful of practices. And some of them are surprisingly easy to copy, even for a family with no fortune at all.
scenes.caption: THE SYSTEMS

scenes.text: Difference number fifteen. Old money families hold family meetings about money.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 15

scenes.text: Many wealthy families hold regular meetings to discuss investments, values, philanthropy and responsibilities. Some have written family constitutions. The Williams Group research suggested that breakdowns in trust and communication within families were among the biggest reasons wealth was lost.
scenes.caption: FAMILY MEETINGS

scenes.text: New money often keeps money secret, even from spouses and children. Then, when wealth is passed on, heirs are unprepared and families fight.
scenes.caption: WHEN COMMUNICATION BREAKS

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Hold a simple family money meeting once or twice a year. Share goals and values, and age appropriate details.
scenes.caption: ONCE OR TWICE A YEAR

scenes.text: A family meeting doesn't need to be formal. It can be a dinner where you share one goal, one decision and one lesson. Older kids can learn how the household budget works. Adult children can learn where important documents are kept. Those simple conversations prevent confusion and conflict later, which is exactly where many family fortunes break down.
scenes.caption: IT CAN BE A DINNER

scenes.text: Difference number sixteen. Old money prepares heirs before giving them money.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 16

scenes.text: The same research found that unprepared heirs were a major cause of lost fortunes. Old money families often teach children about money early, give them responsibilities gradually, and sometimes release inheritances in stages.
scenes.caption: TEACH BEFORE GIVING

scenes.text: Thomas Stanley also found that large ongoing gifts to adult children were linked with those children accumulating less wealth of their own. Preparation matters more than the amount.
scenes.caption: STAGED INHERITANCE

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Teach your kids about money early, let them earn, let them make small mistakes, and give responsibility before giving large sums.
scenes.caption: LET THEM EARN

scenes.text: Some families use what are sometimes called incentive trusts, which release money when heirs reach certain milestones, like finishing school or matching their own earned income. Whether or not you ever set up a trust, the principle is valuable. Money works best when it supports effort and responsibility, rather than replacing them.
scenes.caption: MONEY THAT SUPPORTS EFFORT

scenes.text: Difference number seventeen. Old money gives as a family.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 17

scenes.text: Many old money families run foundations or give together. Philanthropy can unite family members around shared values, teach younger generations about responsibility, and, under US law, offer legal tax benefits.
scenes.caption: GIVING AS A FAMILY

scenes.text: New money is increasingly generous too. Many self made billionaires have pledged to give away large parts of their fortunes. The habit of giving keeps money in perspective.
scenes.caption: SHARED VALUES

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Choose a cause as a family and give together, even small amounts. It builds values that outlast money.
scenes.caption: START SMALL

scenes.text: Andrew Carnegie, one of the richest Americans of his era, famously argued that the man who dies rich dies disgraced, and gave away most of his fortune to libraries, universities and other causes. More recently, the Giving Pledge, started by Warren Buffett and Bill and Melinda French Gates, invites billionaires to commit to giving away the majority of their wealth.
scenes.caption: ANDREW CARNEGIE

scenes.text: Difference number eighteen. Old money holds for decades.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 18

scenes.text: Old money families often keep land, businesses and investments for generations. Long holding periods reduce taxes, trading costs and the risk of emotional mistakes. They let compounding do its work.
scenes.caption: BUY AND KEEP

scenes.text: New money investors may trade more frequently, chasing trends. Research on individual investors, like studies by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean, has found that frequent traders tended to earn lower returns after costs.
scenes.caption: TRADING TOO MUCH

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Buy diversified investments and hold them for the long term. Check them occasionally, not constantly.
scenes.caption: HOLD FOR DECADES

scenes.text: The research by Barber and Odean looked at tens of thousands of household brokerage accounts in the nineteen nineties. The households that traded the most earned noticeably lower returns than the market, largely because of trading costs and poorly timed decisions. Doing less was often the winning strategy.
scenes.caption: DOING LESS WINS

scenes.text: Difference number nineteen. What new money does better.
scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 19

scenes.text: New money has real strengths. Hunger, creativity, risk taking and a willingness to work extremely hard. Ramsey Solutions' study found that most American millionaires were first generation. And UBS has reported that self made entrepreneurs create a large share of new billionaire wealth each year.
scenes.caption: HUSTLE AND REINVENTION
scenes.short_hook: Self made money has one big advantage old money doesn't.

scenes.text: Old money heirs sometimes lose that drive. Without the need to build, some drift. That's one reason fortunes fade. The families that last often find ways to keep entrepreneurship alive in each generation.
scenes.caption: FIRST GENERATION WEALTH

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Keep the hustle of new money. Build skills, take smart risks and create value. Then add the protection habits of old money.
scenes.caption: KEEP THE DRIVE

scenes.text: Think of the immigrant shop owner, the first generation college graduate who starts a company, or the tradesperson who builds a contracting business from a single truck. Their drive, frugality and appetite for work are exactly what old money families try to keep alive in later generations, often without success.
scenes.caption: FIRST GENERATION DRIVE

scenes.text: And difference number twenty. The best approach combines both.

card.title: The best of both
card.sub: build like new, keep like old

scenes.caption: DIFFERENCE 20

scenes.text: Build like new money. Work hard, take smart risks, grow your income and create value. Keep like old money. Spend below your means, diversify, plan for taxes, protect with structure, think long term, and prepare the next generation.
scenes.caption: BUILD LIKE NEW

scenes.text: That combination is exactly what many self made millionaires do. They build with hunger, then protect with discipline. And some of them become the founders of new old money families.
scenes.caption: KEEP LIKE OLD

scenes.text: The lesson for anyone. Ask yourself which side you're stronger on. Building or keeping. Then work on the other side.
scenes.caption: WORK ON THE OTHER SIDE

scenes.text: Picture someone who builds a small business with long hours and smart risks, then pays themselves a modest salary, invests the profits in diversified index funds, writes a will, teaches their kids to work, and talks openly with their family about money. That person is building the first chapter of an old money story.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST CHAPTER

scenes.text: Let's name the classic mistakes that sink new fortunes, so you can avoid them at any level. Mistake one. Upgrading everything at once. A sudden jump in lifestyle locks in high fixed costs that are hard to reverse. Mistake two. Lending or giving money to everyone who asks, without limits. It can drain a fortune and damage relationships at the same time.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 1 AND 2

scenes.text: Mistake three. Investing in friends' businesses or exciting deals without proper due diligence. Mistake four. Ignoring taxes until the bill arrives. And mistake five. Assuming the income will continue forever. Careers end, markets change, and companies fail. Old money families plan as if the good times might not last, which is exactly why theirs often do.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 3, 4 AND 5

scenes.text: The antidote to all five is a pause. When new money arrives, whether it's a big raise, a bonus or an inheritance, many planners suggest parking it somewhere safe for a few months before making big decisions. Time cools emotions and lets a clear plan form. The money will still be there in three months. A rushed decision, on the other hand, can be very hard to undo.
scenes.caption: PAUSE BEFORE YOU SPEND

scenes.text: Why does this matter now? Because America is in the middle of what's often called the great wealth transfer. Research firms like Cerulli Associates have estimated that tens of trillions of dollars will pass from older Americans to heirs and charities over the coming decades. UBS has also reported that inherited wealth is creating a large share of new billionaires.
scenes.query: Older couple handing keys to young adult
scenes.caption: THE GREAT WEALTH TRANSFER

scenes.text: If the old pattern holds, much of that money will be gone within a generation or two. The families who keep it will be the ones with old money habits. Communication, preparation, diversification, spending discipline and long term thinking.
scenes.caption: WHO WILL KEEP IT?

scenes.text: And for families without big inheritances, the same habits can start something new. Every old money family began with someone who built and then protected. That person could be you.
scenes.caption: IT COULD START WITH YOU

scenes.text: So how would an ordinary family start becoming old money, from scratch? Here's a simple thirty year outline.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Starting your own old money family

scenes.text: Years one to ten. Build. Grow your income, live below it, and invest the difference automatically in diversified, low cost funds. Pay off high interest debt. Build an emergency fund. Write a will and name beneficiaries. Teach your kids the basics, like saving, earning and waiting for things they want.
scenes.caption: YEARS 1 TO 10: BUILD

scenes.text: Years eleven to twenty. Grow and protect. Keep raising your savings rate with every raise. Add income producing assets, maybe a rental property or a small business, if they fit your skills. Review insurance and estate plans. Start family money meetings, and give older kids real responsibility for part of their own spending.
scenes.caption: YEARS 11 TO 20: GROW AND PROTECT

scenes.text: Years twenty one to thirty. Keep and pass on. Shift toward preserving wealth, with careful diversification and a sustainable spending rate. Involve adult children in family decisions and philanthropy. Prepare them before passing anything on. By then, you've done what every old money family once did. You built something, and taught the next generation how to keep it.
scenes.caption: YEARS 21 TO 30: KEEP AND PASS ON

scenes.text: From old money, copy these. Live on less than you earn. Build income producing assets. Diversify. Think in decades. Have a will and name beneficiaries. Teach your kids about money. And keep your wealth quiet.
scenes.caption: COPY FROM OLD MONEY

scenes.text: From new money, copy these. Grow your income. Take calculated risks with your career. Build skills that create value. Be willing to start something. And stay hungry. Together, those habits are a powerful combination at any income level.
scenes.caption: COPY FROM NEW MONEY

scenes.text: Question one. Is old money always better with money? No. Plenty of old money families lose their wealth, and plenty of new money builders manage it brilliantly. These are patterns, not rules. The habits matter more than the label.
scenes.caption: IS OLD MONEY BETTER?

scenes.text: Question two. Do I need to be rich to use trusts and estate planning? Not necessarily. A basic will and beneficiary designations are important for almost everyone. Trusts can be useful for families with young children, property in multiple states, or complex situations. An estate planning attorney can help you decide.
scenes.caption: TRUSTS FOR EVERYONE?

scenes.text: Question three. What's the single most important old money habit? Probably spending only part of what your assets earn, and never the principal. That one rule, followed over decades, is how fortunes survive.
scenes.caption: THE MOST IMPORTANT HABIT

scenes.text: Question four. Is quiet luxury just another trend to buy into? It can be. Some brands now sell expensive plain clothing labeled as quiet luxury. That misses the point. The old money idea isn't buying a different look. It's caring less about looks altogether, and putting the money into assets instead.
scenes.caption: QUIET LUXURY AS A TREND

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Assets versus income, generations versus years, diversified versus concentrated, debt as a tool, tax planning, spending rate, and protection.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. Quiet versus loud, quality versus brands, security versus proving, patience versus speed, networks, identity beyond money, and risk appetite.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Family meetings, preparing heirs, philanthropy, long term holding, what new money does better, and the best of both.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.text: Here's what I find most encouraging about this topic. Every old money family, without exception, started with one person who built something and decided to protect it. Their habits weren't secret, and they weren't complicated. Spend less than you earn, own assets, think long term, and teach the next generation. You don't need a famous last name to think like old money, or a startup exit to build like new money. Build like new, keep like old. If you want the full plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments, are you more of a builder or a keeper? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
